**MEMO: GPU Capacity — Buy More or Use What We Have Better?**

**To:** Engineering Team
**From:** Infrastructure Lead
**Re:** Recommendation on our compute capacity decision
**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

Over the past month we've hit inference queue saturation three times, and the natural instinct is to reach for a purchase order. Before we do that, I want to lay out how I'm thinking about the choice between buying additional local hardware and improving utilisation of the eight GPUs we already own, because I think the right answer is more nuanced than either extreme.

Let's start with the economics. Our current fleet is fully depreciated, so its marginal cost is essentially power, cooling, and our time. Every additional GPU we buy carries not just a capital price but a real carrying cost: rack space, maintenance contracts, and the depreciation clock that starts the day the box arrives. Against that, our measured utilisation sits around 40 percent averaged across the fleet, with individual nodes swinging between idle and pegged. That gap is the whole argument. If we could lift average utilisation to 70 percent, we'd effectively add capacity equal to nearly two GPUs without spending capital, and we'd do it with engineering time we were going to spend anyway. The catch, of course, is that utilisation gains are not free. Batching improvements add latency to individual requests. Better scheduling means jobs wait longer for a slot. There is a real trade between throughput and responsiveness, and we need to be honest about where our users feel it.

That brings me to latency. Our most latency-sensitive workload is the interactive assistant path, where p95 response time is already brushing against our 800-millisecond target during peak hours. Squeezing more utilisation out of the fleet by co-locating batch jobs with interactive traffic risks pushing that number over the line, and the reputational cost of a sluggish product is harder to quantify than a GPU invoice but no less real. The right move, I think, is to partition: protect the interactive path with dedicated capacity and aggressive scheduling, and push everything else into a shared pool where high utilisation is acceptable. That gets us most of the efficiency gains without touching the experience our users actually notice.

Reliability cuts the other way. Right now, losing a single node takes out roughly an eighth of our capacity, and our redundancy is thin. Buying more hardware would improve fault tolerance as a side effect, which is genuinely valuable and easy to undervalue. Better utilisation, by contrast, tends to concentrate load and can make failures more visible. If we go the utilisation route, we should pair it with a modest investment in failover tooling so that a dead GPU degrades service gracefully rather than dropping requests. That tooling cost should be counted honestly against the utilisation option.

Then there's opportunity cost, which I think is the decisive factor. The engineering time required to build proper scheduling, batching, and partitioning is time not spent on the model improvements and product features that actually differentiate us. Hardware, once bought, is a solved problem; software for scheduling is an ongoing tax. But the reverse is also true: if we buy hardware to paper over a scheduling problem, we'll be back here in a year, having paid twice for capacity we only half-use. The question is which tax is cheaper and which one compounds.

Finally, reversibility. Buying GPUs is close to irreversible at our scale — resale recovers a fraction of cost, and the capital is gone. Building scheduling and partitioning software is highly reversible: if it turns out we still need hardware after six months of better utilisation, nothing is wasted, because the software makes any future fleet more efficient anyway. When one option is reversible and the other is not, and both plausibly address the problem, the reversible option deserves the first attempt.

So my recommendation: commit the next quarter to the utilisation track. Partition interactive and batch workloads, implement dynamic batching on the two models where it's cheapest, and set a concrete target of 65 percent average utilisation with p95 interactive latency held under 800 milliseconds. Revisit the hardware question at the end of the quarter with real data. If we hit the target and are still saturating, the case for purchase will be strong and well-evidenced. If we miss it, we'll have learned exactly where the ceiling is.

I want to acknowledge the uncertainty here honestly. Our utilisation numbers come from a monitoring setup we've already caught undercounting, and demand forecasts for the next two quarters are soft. It's possible demand growth simply outruns anything scheduling can deliver, and we buy hardware in October anyway. But given the asymmetry — cheap, reversible software work versus expensive, irreversible capital — I'm confident this is the right first move. I'd rather earn the purchase order than guess at it.

Comments welcome before Thursday.

**To:** Engineering Leadership
**From:** Infrastructure Team
**Re:** Recommendation on AI compute capacity for the next two quarters

**Status:** For discussion at Thursday's planning session

---

Over the past month we've been asked, informally but repeatedly, whether we should purchase additional local GPU hardware or focus on extracting more value from the machines we already own. The question sounds simple, but it sits at the intersection of several tensions worth spelling out before we commit money or attention. This memo lays out our thinking and proposes a direction.

The case for buying more hardware is easy to state. Our inference cluster runs hot during working hours, and teams occasionally wait in queue for batch jobs. Every hour a data scientist spends waiting for a training run is an hour of expensive human time spent idle, and that cost dwarfs the amortised cost of a GPU in almost any reasonable accounting. Latency matters here too: interactive experimentation has a qualitatively different character when results come back in minutes rather than hours, and the queue-induced friction is, in our assessment, quietly suppressing experimentation. People don't run the fifth variant of an idea when the first four took all afternoon. That hidden loss of exploration is real, even if it never appears on an invoice.

But the case for better utilisation is stronger than it first appears, and we want to be honest about why. Our own telemetry shows average utilisation around 45% across the fleet, with sharp peaks and long troughs. A meaningful fraction of jobs are small models running on large cards purely because scheduling is coarse-grained. We have not yet implemented fractional GPU allocation, priority preemption for batch workloads, or a simple reservation calendar for the interactive pool. These are weeks of engineering effort, not months, and they would likely raise effective utilisation into the 70–80% range. Buying hardware before doing this work would mean paying twice: once for the machines, and once in the opportunity cost of not building the scheduling discipline we will eventually need regardless. More capacity without better allocation simply reproduces today's inefficiency at a larger scale.

Reliability cuts both ways, and we should be clear-eyed about it. Additional hardware gives us redundancy; if a card fails today, queued work stalls in ways that are visible and occasionally embarrassing. A larger fleet absorbs single-node failures gracefully. On the other hand, our current fleet is young and failure rates have been low, and the operational burden of more machines — driver updates, thermal management, power, and the growing complexity of a heterogeneous estate — is a reliability cost of its own. We would rather operate fewer, well-scheduled machines than more, poorly-scheduled ones.

Reversibility is the final consideration, and it tilts the balance. Hardware purchases are close to irreversible at our scale. Depreciation is fast in this market, resale values for used accelerators are volatile, and a purchase made for this quarter's demand becomes a sunk cost if our workload mix shifts toward hosted APIs or smaller models. Scheduling and allocation work, by contrast, is an investment in capability that pays off under almost any future scenario. If we later do buy hardware, we will buy it with better information and better tooling to exploit it. If we never need to buy, we will have saved a substantial capital outlay. The option value of waiting, while we improve utilisation, is significant and largely free.

Our recommendation, therefore, is to defer hardware purchase for two quarters and instead fund a focused utilisation initiative: fractional allocation, workload prioritisation, and better observability into who is waiting for what and why. We would pair this with a modest, capped budget for short-term cloud burst capacity to cover genuine peak overflow, which is fully reversible and gives us a pressure valve while the scheduling work lands. At the end of that period, we should revisit the purchase question with real data rather than the anecdotal queue complaints that prompted this discussion.

We want to acknowledge the uncertainty in this position honestly. Our utilisation figures come from coarse instrumentation and may understate true contention; if the real number is already above 60%, the case for buying sooner strengthens considerably. There is also a risk that the scheduling work proves harder than estimated, and that we spend two quarters optimising when we should have been shipping models. The case for buying more hardware is the obvious one: it works. When we're queue-starved at peak hours, latency for interactive requests degrades from our target of under 400 milliseconds to well over two seconds, and that degradation is felt directly by users and indirectly by our own developers, who have started scheduling batch jobs at odd hours to avoid contention. Adding capacity removes the problem rather than managing it. It's also fast, at least in procurement terms — we can have machines racked and serving traffic within a couple of weeks, whereas the software-side improvements we'd need to make are measured in months of engineering time.

But that speed comes at a price that's easy to underestimate. The capital outlay is significant, and more importantly it's largely irreversible. GPUs depreciate quickly, resale markets are thin, and if our workload profile shifts — say, if we move more inference to a hosted API for the long tail of low-value requests, or if model efficiency improvements cut our per-request compute by half — we'll be holding hardware we can't easily convert back into budget. That irreversibility is the strongest argument against buying now. An option we can't undo should demand a higher bar of confidence than one we can.

The alternative — improving utilisation — is less glamorous but the numbers are compelling. Our average utilisation sits around 40%, with peaks near 95% and long troughs overnight. That gap is where the opportunity lives. Better batching, more aggressive quantisation for models that tolerate it, a proper scheduling layer that lets batch work fill the valleys, and caching for our most common request patterns could plausibly get us to 65–70% effective utilisation. That's the equivalent of adding half again our current capacity, at a fraction of the cost, and — crucially — it's reversible. If a technique doesn't work, we turn it off. If priorities change, the engineering effort transfers to whatever we run next. We're buying options, not inventory.

Pushing utilisation up means accepting queues, and queues mean tail latency, and our worst p99 numbers during the last load test came precisely from aggressive batching. Reliability cuts both ways, too. More hardware means more redundancy and gentler operating conditions for each machine, which should reduce failure rates. Our current fleet is small enough that one person can hold its topology in their head; doubling it changes that.

**Re:** Recommendation on our compute capacity decision for the next two quarters

**Summary**

We recommend that we spend the next quarter aggressively improving utilisation of our existing hardware before committing to any new purchases. The case for buying more capacity is real, but it is not yet strong enough to justify the cost, and the option to buy later does not expire. The case for better utilisation, by contrast, is concrete, cheap, and largely reversible if it fails.

**Where we stand**

Our current cluster runs at roughly 40–45% average utilisation, with sharp peaks around batch jobs and long idle stretches overnight and on weekends. At the same time, individual teams are queuing for access, and at least two projects have quietly deprioritised model work because they could not get reliable time on the machines. This combination — idle capacity alongside frustrated demand — is the clearest signal that our problem is allocation, not raw supply. If we were running at 85% with queues still forming, the conversation would be different.
